titre: The fat that no vitamin could replace
accroche: Around 1929, a couple of biochemists strip rats of all fat, vitamins included, and uncover a disease that current theory never predicted.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the late 1920s, at the University of Minnesota, the dominant theory about dietary fat held to two roles: an energy reserve, and a carrier for the fat-soluble vitamins A and D. As long as those two needs were met some other way, fat itself should be superfluous. George Burr and Mildred Burr, a couple of biochemists, decided to test this idea to the letter. They built a diet for rats entirely free of fat, using sucrose and casein purified to remove the slightest trace of it, to which they added vitamins A, D and E in sufficient amounts, so as to isolate a single variable: fat itself.

## A disease the theory never predicted

If the prevailing theory had been complete, these rats should have fared normally. Instead, they wasted away in a methodical pattern. Their skin turned scaly, their tails became inflamed and then crusted with scales, their fur fell out in patches, their growth stopped, and they died, three to four months after the weight loss began. Autopsies revealed kidney damage. The Burrs published this description in 1929 in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, under a title that announced the conclusion outright: a new deficiency disease, produced by the rigid exclusion of fat from the diet.

## One single molecule, not fat in general

The question remained whether it was fat as a whole that was missing, or just one of its components. The following year, the Burrs answered by experiment: a few drops of olive oil, lard, or linseed oil were enough to cure the syndrome, and the active ingredient common to these three sources turned out to be linoleic acid. Saturated fatty acids, by contrast, such as stearic acid or palmitic acid, had no effect at all, even given generously. Fat, then, is not interchangeable: a single fatty acid, one the rat's body cannot make on its own, is indispensable to it.

The reach of this finding goes well beyond the starved laboratory rat. It forces a reclassification of dietary fat itself: no longer just an energy reserve or a carrier for other nutrients, it is also, through at least one of its components, a nutrient in its own right, on the same footing as a vitamin, one the body can only get from food. The linoleic acid identified by the Burrs would later be placed in the family now called omega-6; a second essential fatty acid, linolenic acid, its omega-3 counterpart, would be identified afterward. Two decades before those families got their names, a couple of biochemists had already proven, on rats stripped of everything, that a fat could be missing exactly the way a vitamin could.

repere.texte: Stripped of all fat, the Burrs' rats lost weight and died three to four months later; a few drops of linoleic acid were enough to cure them, while saturated fatty acids, such as stearic or palmitic acid, had no effect at all.
repere.source: Based on Burr, G.O. and Burr, M.M., Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1929 and 1930, republished as JBC Classics, 2012

carte.punch: A couple of biochemists proved that a fat could go missing, exactly like a vitamin.
carte.idee: Around 1929, George and Mildred Burr strip rats of all fat, vitamins included. The rats waste away regardless: scaly skin, a scaly tail, death after a few months. A single fatty acid, linoleic acid, cures the syndrome; saturated fatty acids change nothing.

quiz.question: Why does the diet designed by the Burrs show that it is the lack of fat, and not of fat-soluble vitamins, that makes the rats sick?
choix: Because vitamins A, D and E were added to the diet, in sufficient amounts
Because the rats received twice the usual amount of vitamins
Because the diet contained no vitamins at all, on purpose
Because the rats were compared to wild rats living outdoors
quiz.explication: The Burrs' diet added vitamins A, D and E in sufficient amounts, which isolated a single variable: fat itself. The rats still fell ill, which disproved the idea that fat was only a carrier for those vitamins.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What symptoms do rats deprived of fat develop, according to the Burrs' papers?
choix: Scaly skin, an inflamed and then scale-crusted tail, hair loss
No visible symptoms before sudden death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rats deprived of all fat develop scaly skin, a tail that becomes inflamed and then crusts with scales, patchy hair loss, stopped growth, and die, three to four months after the weight loss began, with kidney damage found on autopsy.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which fatty acid cures the syndrome described by the Burrs, and which one has no effect?
choix: Linoleic acid cures it; saturated fatty acids such as stearic acid have no effect
Saturated fatty acids cure it; linoleic acid has no effect
Every fatty acid, saturated or not, cures the syndrome equally
No fatty acid cures the syndrome, only vitamins do
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A few drops of linoleic acid, present in olive oil, lard, or linseed oil, are enough to cure the syndrome. Saturated fatty acids, such as stearic or palmitic acid, have no effect at all, even given generously.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the Burrs' discovery change the way dietary fat is understood?
choix: It shows that at least one component of fat is an indispensable nutrient the body cannot make itself
It shows that fat has no nutritional use of its own
It shows that only fat-soluble vitamins matter within fat
It shows that all fatty acids are strictly equivalent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Before the Burrs, fat was seen only as an energy reserve and a carrier for vitamins A and D. Their discovery forces a reclassification: at least one of its components, linoleic acid, is a nutrient in its own right, as indispensable as a vitamin.
